ABSTRACT. Let (X,∥·∥X),(Y,∥·∥Y) be normed spaces with dim(X) = n. Bourgain’s almost extension theorem

2. EXTENSION VERSUS ALMOST EXTENSION
By proving Theorem 1, Bourgain’s achievement was not limited to merely establishing its statement.
It contains the noteworthy conceptual realization that his formulation of the almost extension problem
overcomes a barrier that previously precluded certain applications. Theorem 1 shows that by relaxing the
traditional requirement that the restriction of F to N coincides with f to the weaker requirement that the
restriction of F to N is close to f , it is possible ensure that F is O(1)-Lipschitz; this can fail badly if one
insists that F extends f , namely, in that case the Lipschitz constant must sometimes tend to ∞with n.
2


At the same time, some important applications necessitate that F is O(1)-Lipschitz, and they persist if F
is O(1)-Lipschitz yet only sufﬁciently close to f on N, as demonstrated decisively in [Bou87].
The input of the classical Lipschitz extension problem is two metric spaces (M,dM),(Z,dZ), as well
as a subset Ω⊆M. The goal is to determine if there is K ∈[1,∞) such that for every Lipschitz function
f : Ω→Z there is a function F : M →Z that extends f , i.e., F(ω) = f (ω) for all ω ∈Ω, and such that
∥F∥Lip ⩽K ∥f ∥Lip. Here, and in what follows, ∥·∥Lip denotes the Lipschitz constant. Let e(M,Ω;Z) denote
the inﬁmum over those K for which the above extension phenomenon holds, with the convention that
e(M,Ω;Z) = ∞if there is no such K . Write e(M;Z) = supΩ⊆M e(M,Ω;Z). Also, denote by e(M,Ω) the
supremum of e(M,Ω;Y) as Y ranges over all Banach spaces, and deﬁne e(M) = supΩ⊆M e(M,Ω).
Finding geometric conditions on the triple (M,Ω,Z) which ensure that e(M,Ω;Z) < ∞, and moreover
obtaining upper and lower bounds on e(M,Ω;Z), are important questions with applications in several
areas. The techniques that were developed to extend Lipschitz functions exhibit a rich interplay between
this area and other mathematical disciplines; see the monograph [BB12] for an indication of (part of) the
many results along these lines that have been obtained over the past century.
While e(M;Ω) is deﬁned in terms of extension of mappings that can take values in all possible Banach
spaces, it has an intrinsic geometric characterization [Koz05, BB07, Oht09, AP20]. We will next explain a
generalization of this fact that applies to (but is more general than) the almost extension setting of The-
orem 1; this will clarify the geometric task at hand, and will also be valuable for the proof of Theorem 4.

The above discussion demonstrates that even in the seemingly “nice” setting of ﬁnite dimensional
normed (even Euclidean) spaces2, one cannot hope to be able to extend any 1-Lipschitz mapping to
a mapping whose Lipschitz constant does not tend to ∞with the dimension (moreover, the rate must
sometime be of power-type). In contrast, in Theorem 1 Bourgain speciﬁes a ﬁrm upper bound L that the
Lipschitz constant of F must not exceed, and shows that this is achievable by no longer insisting that F
extends f . Having such control on the Lipschitz constant of F is important for certain applications, most
notably the alternative tradeoff of Theorem 1 is used crucially in the proof of Bourgain’s discretization
theorem [Bou87], which is a quantitative version of an important rigidity theorem of Ribe [Rib76].
When one is given a discretely-deﬁned 1-Lipschitz mapping f , it is often desirable to obtain a mapping
F that “mimics” f yet is deﬁned on the entire ambient normed space, so as to be able to apply continuous
methods, e.g. using differentiation or harmonic analysis. Any such reasoning that needs dimension-
independent bounds on the derivatives of F requires good control on ∥F∥Lip. The proof of Ribe’s theorem
in [Bou87] would utterly fail if the norm of the derivative of F were unbounded as n →∞, because Ribe’s
theorem is all about dimension-independent bounds (its conclusion concerns the ﬁnite representability
of an inﬁnite dimensional Banach space). At the same time, by [Bou87] the desired statement (Ribe’s
theorem, and even a quantitative version thereof) follows if F is sufﬁciently close to f on the net N
(per the conclusion of Theorem 1), provided that f is O(1)-bi-Lipschitz, and N is ﬁne enough, i.e., ε is
sufﬁciently small (the requirement of [Bou87] is ε ⩽exp(−exp(O(n))), which remains the best known
bound in full generality; ﬁnding the optimal asymptotic behavior here is a fascinating open question;
see [GNS12, Ost13, LN13, HLN16, HN19]). Other applications of Bourgain’s almost extension theorem
appear in [Bou87, GNS12, NR17, NS20], some of which build on its simpliﬁed proof in [Beg99] (but we
checked that they could be deduced also using the original proof in [Bou87]); not all of these applications
belong to the above framework, e.g. [NR17, Corollary 22] is a statement in approximation theory.
Beyond his demonstration of the highly signiﬁcant application to Ribe’s rigidity theorem, Bourgain
took note of the potential of the aforementioned “twist” in Theorem 1 on the classical Lipschitz extension
problem, wherein one can specify the desired bound on ∥F∥Lip, by stating on page 158 of [Bou87] that
the existence of such a mapping “may already have considerable implications.” He proceeded to further
illustrate this by deducing Theorem 9 below on almost ellipsoidal sections. It is beneﬁcial to recall this
speciﬁc application here because of its direct relevance to the present work, namely this is how a power-
type impossibility result in the context of Theorem 1 is obtained in [Bou87].

former means that infa∈N dM(x,a) ⩽ε for every x ∈M, and the latter means that dM(a,b) ⩾δ for every

Abstract: Let (X,∥·∥X),(Y,∥·∥Y) be normed spaces with dim(X) = n. Bourgain’s almost extension theorem asserts that for any ε > 0, if N is an ε-net of the unit sphere of X and f : N →Y is 1-Lipschitz, then there exists an O(1)-Lipschitz F : X →Y such that ∥F(a) −f (a)∥Y ≲nε for all a ∈N. We prove that this is optimal up to lower order factors, i.e., sometimes maxa∈N ∥F(a)−f (a)∥Y ≳n1−o(1)ε for every O(1)-Lipschitz F : X →Y. This improves Bourgain’s lower bound of maxa∈N ∥F(a)−f (a)∥Y ≳nc ε for some 0 < c < 1 2. If X = ℓn 2 , then the approximation in the almost extension theorem can be improved to maxa∈N ∥F(a)−f (a)∥Y ≲pnε. We prove that this is sharp, i.e., sometimes maxa∈N ∥F(a)−f (a)∥Y ≳pnε for every O(1)-Lipschitz F : ℓn 2 →Y.
